extracted.intended_audience: farmers, rural homeowners, builders and designers of domestic ventilation and water-supply systems
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for designing and evaluating ventilation and domestic water-supply systems for farmhouses, stables, and small rural properties. Covers stove ventilation, inlet/outlet sizing and placement, stable ventilation, economic trade-offs, quantities and peak rates of household water use, fire-stream requirements, rainwater and stream storage calculations, and remedies for deficient wells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stove-floor damper arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: When the fire is burning freely, the damper at C is closed, and ventilation is secured through the stove, the damper at B being open. When the damper at B is closed and the fire checked, then the damper at C may be opened and the impure air drawn up the chimney from the level of the floor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dampers to control whether stove ventilation draws air from near the floor (for removing polluted air) or through the stove itself; operate dampers depending on fire conditions to create the desired draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheet-iron casing with independent flue
rubrics_metrics.description: Surround the stove with a sheet-iron casing, the top of the casing having a pipe leading into the chimney independently from the stovepipe. If the damper in the flue from the casing be opened partly, a strong draft along the floor and into this casing will be developed and the foul air thereby discharged into the chimney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The casing radiates heat like the stove but opening the casing-flue draws foul air along the floor; regulate the damper carefully because it is easy to carry away all heat from the stove with this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stove jacket with outside-air underfeed
rubrics_metrics.description: Surround the stove with a sheet-iron jacket extending from the floor to about six feet above; carry a pipe from the outside air up through the floor directly under the stove. By regulating the damper in this pipe the supply of fresh warmed air entering the room can be regulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide doors in the casing for tending the fire and allow the option of heating room air instead of outside air; regulate dampers to control fresh-air intake and avoid unnecessary heat loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ceiling register outlets for polluted air
rubrics_metrics.description: A most objectionable method of providing an outlet for polluted air from a room is to have a register in the ceiling with the ostensible purpose of warming the room above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceiling registers can allow kitchen odors to permeate upper rooms (example: odors of cabbage, onions, codfish); avoid using ceiling registers as outlets for polluted air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size of fresh-air inlet — theoretical rule
rubrics_metrics.description: At least twenty-four square inches sectional area should be allowed as an inlet for each person, so that one square foot is required for six persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a theoretical requirement and often more area than obtained in practice; use as a conservative guideline for limiting air velocity and preventing objectionable drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size of fresh-air inlet — practical (with combustion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking into account the necessary air required by lamps or gas burners, the inlet flue should have at least ten square inches area for each person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ordinary living rooms a single register of this area will often provide necessary air; adjust based on fuel-burning devices in the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of outlet flue (passive inlet)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an outlet is cut into the wall and a flue carried up through the roof, the flue should be preferably near the floor and on the side of the room opposite the window or inlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With this arrangement air currents flow diagonally across the room from ceiling to floor, renewing all air particles except those directly over the outlet; it improves cross-room air renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of inlet/outlet for mechanical supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the air is introduced mechanically, it is better to have the inlet and outlet on the same side, so that the entering air is shot in at the top, flowing across the room, then sinking and coming back, just below the point where it entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design mechanical inlets/outlets to create controlled circulation patterns rather than short-circuiting the flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply house ventilation principles to stables
rubrics_metrics.description: All that has been said on the subject of ventilation in houses applies equally well to the ventilation of stables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a flue to carry foul air up through the roof, fresh-air inlets in the outer walls on both sides, and control all openings carefully; avoid old underground stable designs that exclude outside air and crowd animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of openings when ventilation installed
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as regular inlets and outlets are provided, all other openings ought to be rigidly closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closing unintended openings ensures warmed pure air is admitted only at intended points and preserves the full value of the heating and ventilation system; especially important in barns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wall and ceiling construction for ventilated buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: Walls and ceiling should not merely be tight in themselves, but they should be double, and the strictest attention paid to limiting the amount of heat lost by radiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board studding and joists inside and out; fill space with shavings, straw, dry moss or similar fibrous material; ensure outside sheathing is water-tight and roof is tight to prevent rot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: poorly-built drafty vs air-tight ventilated structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice between a poorly built, loose-jointed structure without artificial ventilation and a well-built, air-tight structure, with ample ventilating pipes, carefully and intelligently planned and built.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly built structures may be healthy in pure-air terms but drafty and uncomfortable; well-built air-tight houses are more expensive but insure lasting health, comfort and easier heating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern tendency: running water inside the farmhouse
rubrics_metrics.description: Farmhouses are increasingly being provided with running water in the kitchen sink and with a bathroom containing all the modern conveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running water improves comfort and health but costs money for pipeline and plumbing fixtures; maintain warm pipes in winter to avoid freezing and damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate average water consumption per person
rubrics_metrics.description: Average in a house having a kitchen sink and a bath-room ... a fair estimate of the water used would be twenty-five gallons per head per day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply by maximum number of persons likely present, and add water used for barn and yard if supplied from same source; actual per-head use varies widely (7–59 gallons) by habits and fixtures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for water used outside (stables, yard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amount of water used in the barn is even more than that used in the house, depending on uses like washing cans, aerators, washing harnesses, washing concrete floors, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate external uses separately and add to household demand when sizing supply and storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish total daily quantity from maximum rate (peak flow)
rubrics_metrics.description: The total quantity of water used per day governs reservoir size/yield, while the rate at which water is used governs pipe/faucet/pump capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design piping and pumps for probable simultaneous usage (example: three faucets running concurrently require delivery of three quarts in ten seconds — ~6000 gallons/day equivalent); size reservoir for 24-hour totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for variation in maximum rates (wash-days, seasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Monday (wash-day) about half as much water again is used; in hot weather more water is used for bathing and laundry; in cold weather leaving faucets trickling to prevent freezing may double consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a margin (e.g., double estimated daily needs) to meet excessive daily consumption and seasonal extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire-stream capacity and storage for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A good-sized fire stream delivers about 150 gallons per minute; for a house in flames, four streams are none too many, so rate should be at least 600 gallons per minute or nearly a million gallons per day and an hour's fire uses 36,000 gallons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on springs or tanks, provide ~36,000 gallons storage and pipes large enough to deliver 600 gpm; for distances up to 500 ft a four-inch pipe may suffice, longer distances require larger pipes (six- or eight-inch) because of friction. Consider costs and insurance trade-offs; option to build elevated tank instead of large mains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rain-water supply sizing — roof catchment computation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordinary house has about 1000 sq ft area; average monthly rainfall ~3.75 inches gives about 80 gallons/day from 1000 sq ft. For a family of five requiring 250 gallons/day (doubled for emergencies), compute three-month needs and subtract two-thirds of average three-month rainfall to size tank (example leads to ~13,250 gallons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a three-month period to average rainfall variability; base rainfall estimates on local averages; design tanks to tide over likely dry periods — typical recommendation is about two months' supply or as computed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservoir sizing on small streams — watershed runoff fraction
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining quantity from a small stream the watershed area answers like roof area, but only a fraction of rainfall reaches streams — perhaps one-half on large streams, as little as 20% on sandy soils; in winter most rainfall reaches streams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make reservoir large enough to furnish water from June to September without rain; three months' supply (example ~45,000 gallons) usually ample; account for evaporation (~1.5 ft over summer) and allow sufficient depth (recommend at least 10 ft) to avoid stagnation and reduced quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for deficient well supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: If a dug well runs dry it may be remedied by running out pipe drains in different directions surrounded with gravel, by sinking the well deeper, or by driving pipe in the bottom to find artesian water. For driven wells use a deep-well pump or use air pressure to force water to the tank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose remedy based on geology and well depth: drains suit shallow sand/gravel wells (trenches at right angles to groundwater flow); deepening may reach porous strata; deep-well pumps (valve A submerged, valve B on pump rod) can lift water from hundreds of feet; air-blower (compressed air) can force water up when an engine is available.
